And he was inflamed with wrath,
and he obtained a letter from the Caliph to the governor of Egypt,
to send him the bones of Nestorius in a casket to Baghdad,
so that he might bury them in the Church of Kokhe.
Now a certain monk of the Nestorians, wishing to remove the reproach from their party,
and to show that it was not Nestorius who was being mocked and stoned by the Jacobites,
said:
"One of the holy Apostles told me in a dream of the night
that this is an error,
and the bones of Nestorius are not there,
nor does any man know his grave."
And thus Gabriel the physician was dissuaded from bringing the bones from Egypt.
After {OCR?} Harun al-Rashid, his son Muhammad al-Amin [ruled] four years and seven months.
This [caliph] stopped the building of Herakleia, which his father had been building.
And he brought up the artisans from Callinicus to Baghdad,
and also the money and the household of his brother al-Ma'mun, whom he had made king over Khorasan.
And in the year 1121,
(1121 of the Greeks,
810 of our Lord), al-Amin and al-Ma'mun began to quarrel with one another,
the beginning of the evil coming from al-Amin,
because he was wanton and profligate,
and did not give his brother the money that his father had bestowed upon him,
but seized for himself the whole allowance of his brother,
and also sent after him cunningly in order to seize him.
And he, when he realized his deceit,
did not come.
Then many rebels appeared.
A man whose name was Amr (or Umar?),
who on account of the murders he had committed in Samosata
was imprisoned in Callinicus,
killed the keeper of the prison,
and fled to Samosata.
And he killed the emir on whose account he had been imprisoned,
and plundered the merchants,
and gathered an army to himself,
and began raiding, killing, and plundering in Palestine,
and he also destroyed the army that came against him with Sulayman the general.
And another rebel who was in Armenia, whose name was Nasr, came to Umar,
and joined with him,
and they began the destruction of the world.
Now al-Amin sent Ali the general with thirty thousand against his brother al-Ma'mun,
while al-Ma'mun sent Tahir the general with four thousand.
And they met one another on the river of Balkh,
and Ali was defeated,
and most of his forces were drowned in the river.
